newsitem.title: CHINA: China burns heroin as object lesson in history.
newsitem.headline: China burns heroin as object lesson in history.

text.p: Beijing recast history as object lesson on Sunday, burning 150kg (330 pounds) of heroin in a ceremony to mark China's destruction of 20,000 opium chests in 1839 -- which sparked an Opium War and Hong Kong's colonisation.
Chinese officials set five kerosene-drenched biers of heroin alight in the port city of Humen and the inferno forced several thousand onlookers to jump back from searing heat and flames.
Palls of black smoke trailed from the site for nearly an hour and were visible for km (miles).

"This ceremony is very important to me because we are remembering an heroic deed in the past and we are destroying drugs at the same time," said Shao Ji An, 22, a mechanic who attended the event with his brother and girl friend.

"We are remembering how Britain stole Hong Kong from a weak and corrupt Chinese government. We are proud that the British are leaving and that Hong Kong will be part of China again at the end of this month."
Britain hands Hong Kong back to China at the stroke of midnight on June 30 after a 156-year colonial interlude which had its beginnings in the opium trade.

Britain foisted opium onto China beginning in the 18th century in an effort to earn cash to offset massive imports of tea and silk. Beijing banned the drug trade in 1796 but London ignored the prohibition.
The Emporer sent emissary Lin Zexu to the southern port city of Guangzhou in 1839 with orders to stamp out the illicit trade in opium flourishing there.
Lin surrounded the British in Guangzhou and captured the 20,000 chests of opium, each containing about 70 kg of the drug.
He transported the cache to the Pearl River port of Humen and destroyed it on the site of Sunday's ceremony where there is also an opium museum.
In retaliation the British sent an expeditionary force to China which gained concessionary trade and territorial agreements, among them, in 1841, control over Hong Kong "in perpetuity".
"Perpetuity" ends this month as a result of subsequent agreement over Hong Kong between China and Britain in 1983.
The heroin burned in Humen on Sunday was captured by Chinese government officials in a series of raids.

"All 150 kilograms of heroin was imported to China by foreign drug dealers from the Golden Triangle (a border area where Laos, Thailand and Burma meet)," a representative of the Guangzhou Anti-Drug Commission told Reuters.
China regularly imposes the death penalty on drug traffickers.

Western officials say there is evidence that the country has a huge drug problem which included the use of Golden Triangle heroin and methamphetamine derivatives produced in laboratories in southern China.

An honour-guard of Chinese People's Liberation Army soldiers guarded the heroin in Humen on Sunday as several hundred school children listened to official speeches emphasising the cnnnection between Britain, opium, imperialism and Hong Kong.

"I have brought my daughter here to learn what Britain and America did to China, to learn that they brought the evil of opium to our people to make money off our misery," said one middle-aged man in Humen who refused to give his name.

"If you are British or American you must be ashamed of your history, ashamed of what you did to China. We resisted as best we could but you made war on us. Now we are stronger than Britain and soon we will be stronger than America."
